cards.text: Paul is writing to the church in Corinth. He's just told them his heart is wide open, and he's asked them to open theirs too. Now he gives them a command: "Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers."
Then he backs it up with questions. "For what partnership can righteousness have with wickedness? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?"

cards.question: Righteousness and wickedness. Light and darkness. Why does Paul put these pairs side by side?

answers.text: They are opposites that don't mix
They work best as a team
They are two names for one thing

cards.text: Paul's stacking up these questions like cookies on a tray, and friend, he is NOT slowing down. Next he asks what harmony there is between Christ and Belial.

cards.question: Paul asks what harmony there is between Christ and Belial. True or false: he's pairing them as partners who work together.

cards.text: He asks what a believer has in common with an unbeliever. Then one more: what agreement can there be between the temple of God and idols?

cards.question: Then Paul says something surprising. What does he say is the temple of the living God?

cards.text: WE are the temple, friend, and I spent years in a junk drawer that NOBODY ever called holy. Then Paul backs it up with what God has said.

cards.question: Paul backs it up with what God has said. True or false: God promises to dwell with His people and walk among them.

cards.text: God's words keep going: "I will be their God, and they will be My people." And the next line from the Lord starts with "Therefore."

cards.question: After that "Therefore," what does the Lord call His people to do?

answers.text: Come out from among them and be separate
Stay among them and be their light
Go up to My temple and be cleansed

cards.question: The Lord also says to touch no unclean thing. True or false: He promises He will receive them.

cards.text: Then Paul quotes the Lord Almighty one more time. And friend, this one's a promise.

cards.question: What does the Lord Almighty say He will be to His people?
And the Lord Almighty says they will be His ___ and ___.

cards.text: So Paul wraps it up, and he calls them beloved. Since we have these promises, he says, let's get cleaned up.

cards.question: True or false: Paul says to cleanse ourselves only from what defiles the body.
Paul says that as we cleanse ourselves, we're perfecting ___ in the fear of God.

findings.problem: Belial appears with no word on who Belial is. The text never says who Belial is, and Easton's treats the name as meaning 'worthlessness', later used as a name for Satan. Two rules pull in different directions here. The new-people rule asks for a simple identification. 'Leave open what the text leaves open' and the dictionary pop-up rule point toward saying nothing.
findings.question: When a passage names a figure like Belial that the passage itself never explains, should Papa Dorin identify him on the card (for example 'Belial, a name for Satan', with an outside reference), or leave it to the dictionary pop-up?

findings.problem: The question opens with 'Then Paul says something surprising.' Calling the answer surprising steers the baker away from the expected answer, 'The building in Jerusalem', which rules out a wrong answer in the setup.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The junk drawer joke doesn't land cleanly. Paul says believers are God's temple, and the punchline sets that against a drawer nobody called holy. The two images don't share an action, and the line leaves it unclear whether Papa Dorin is putting himself in the 'we' that is the temple. A stranger would likely say 'huh?'.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: Six verses are stretched to 18 cards. Single verses are split into back-to-back questions (cards 11–12 on 6:17, cards 14–15 on 6:18, cards 17–18 on 7:1), and card 9's question repeats card 8's setup word for word ('Paul backs it up with what God has said'). The stop feels padded to reach the target size.

rule.text: A short passage does what it can. Never force it to fill a stop.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin's humor is thin across the walkthrough. Most story cards (1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 16) are plain retelling. The joke on card 4 is mild, and card 8's joke doesn't land. Lines like 'And friend, this one's a promise' read like a pleasant dad, not a laugh-out-loud storyteller.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
